reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This study focuses on detecting sleep apnea-related respiratory events through the use of a deep learning approach and up to 7 PSG overnight signals (plus data from EEG, EOG, and EMG). The topic is of interest for sleep research, the objectives are well-proposed, and the manuscript is well-written. The authors establish that their approach is useful in sleep apnea detection, mainly because of its ability to properly differentiate the several types of respiratory events (including a new event type), thus covering a gap in the related literature. Despite the interest of the proposal, it is my opinion that several major and minor issues should be addressed prior to the publication of the manuscript:
Major issues:
1/ Apneic event length is 10 seconds or more. Therefore, the frequency associated with their occurrence is below 0.1 Hz. Accordingly, respiratory signals being filtered between 0.1 Hz and 4 Hz are losing very important information. Several studies report that the most useful sleep apnea-related information in respiratory signals is below 0.1 Hz. It is my opinion that filtering should be changed to between 0.025 Hz and 4 Hz to improve the performance of the model, which is high but not impressive.
2/ I understand the advantages of the current proposal regarding previous approaches. However, it is my opinion that the manuscript fails to compare the diagnostic performance (not the scoring performance) with that reached by many other proposals. There exist previous studies using thousands of subjects but only using single channels like SpO2 that reach diagnostic performances that cannot be seen as inferior to those reported here using 7 + 3 signals. As diagnosis is the major conceptual goal of these automated approaches, the authors should compare and discuss these results with other relevant proposals in this particular task.
3/ As there are deep learning solutions that do not require an equal sample rate for the signals, and 8 Hz is below the sampling rate recommended by the AASM for respiratory signals, this choice should be justified and acknowledged as a limitation of the study.
4/ I think that the choice of the particular deep learning architecture should be justified and discussed. The existence of literature pointing to CNNs as reaching higher performances than RNNs, even in tasks involving signal processing (time series), justifies clearly explaining the reasons behind the choice of the deep learning architecture (which in this case includes a combination of both approaches via ResNet).
5/ The intra-class correlation coefficient is better suited than Pearson’s correlation to measure agreement between different scorers (with the predicted AHI being one of them).
Minor issues:
- "To simplify any annotated mixed apneas were labelled as OA due to there being an effort to breathe during the event." It is my opinion that this is not a simplification but a limitation (probably due to an unavoidable class imbalance concerning this type of event)
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors present an assessment of a new automatic sleep disordered breathing event detector (ABED) for identifying respiratory events in sleep disordered breathing. They report that generally the ABED performs as well as individual expert scores, particularly for obstructive apneic events. Data from a number of different, existing cohorts were used to train and validate the ABED, which is a strength of the study.
The potential of this is that the very rapid inference time (14 seconds per average PSG is cited) can increase efficiency and scope of sleep apnea testing.
A number of possible areas for clinical translation are given. I think the most attractive is in easily identifying endotypes of obstructive sleep apnea. Endotypic traits have been proposed for use in selecting patients that might benefit preferentially from a range of non-CPAP alternative therapies including oral appliances, hypoglossal nerve stimulation, supplemental oxygen, and pharmacotherapy. Given there is currently a one-size-fits-all management approach that predominates where CPAP is first line treatment for almost all patients. Accurately identifying patients likely to respond to alternatives to CPAP to avoid a trial and error approach to alternatives would be a major advance. Systems to identify endotypes from routine PSG signals with automated modelling have been developed and some are referenced here (21-25). However, the authors have not referenced further work that has demonstrated some of these systems are highly accurate in predicting, for example, oral appliance treatment outcomes in obstructive sleep apnea (see Dutta et al, J Clin Sleep Med 2022), or that combine clinical data and models from PSG data (see Eckert et al, Sleep 2024;47 (Suppl 1): A257) to identify successful candidates for Oral Appliance Therapy (and vice versa). The authors assert that the addition of “apnotyping” via probabilistic detection of event subtypes within each majority class could benefit sleep apnea endotyping. It remains an open question whether the ABED will be as effective as these methods in clinical practice as this should be acknowledged in the limitations. Further research is also needed to demonstrate if endotypes are useful in predicting which patients are at risk of adverse health consequences of OSA. This is beyond the scope of the current study.
The authors also do not reference previous work on the significance of isolated respiratory events without arousals or desaturations (IRE). Previous work has shown non-apneic REs without cortical arousal or desaturation are associated with significant respiratory and heart rate changes. And, that optimal CPAP and the reduction of resistive load are associated with the normalization of heart rate indicating potential clinical benefit (for example see Sankari et al, Sleep 2016 ;40:zsw024). Easy identification of these events would be useful but is not a novel finding.
There are a number of other limitations I feel need to be considered in addition to those given in the Discussion. As the authors point out in the Introduction, a number of novel metrics taken from the PSG have been identified that have shown to be better predictors of downstream consequences of OSA than the AHI. These include hypoxic burden and a number of metrics derived from heart rates. Further, the intensity of arousals from events are also likely to be clinically significant. It does not appear that the ABED identifies any of these metrics. Consequently, the value of the ABED in identifying which patients may benefit long-term from therapy is uncertain. Sleep studies also require scoring of sleep stages and identification of arousals due to limb movements or that occur spontaneously. I presume the ABED would need to be utilised in addition to automatic scoring software for these features.
Overall, the paper presents a potentially useful addition to automate the scoring of sleep-disordered breathing events that will likely be of value in sleep medicine.

detectable even after applying a 0.1 Hz high-pass filter, since the base breathing
frequencies (typically ~0.2–0.4 Hz) are still present.

most respiratory channels (except nasal flow), whereas MESA and CFS did not apply

bias in model training, we chose a conservative high-pass cutoff of 0.1 Hz. This tradeoff

We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding diagnostic performance.
We agree that comparing our model’s diagnostic utility with simpler approaches is
necessary to contextualize its relevance and impact.
Indeed, previous studies have demonstrated strong diagnostic performance using
single-channel inputs such as SpO2 [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-

valuable - especially in population-level screening contexts.

have been increasingly criticized as insufficient for characterizing apnea severity and
guiding personalized treatment. Our model leverages multichannel PSG data to provide

hypopnea, and isolated respiratory events), and the ability to inform apnea endotyping.

characterizes the temporal structure and type of respiratory disturbances, which are
more closely associated with physiological burden and clinical outcomes. Several
studies emphasize the importance of phenotyping sleep apnea patients beyond the AHI

not easily captured by single-channel or threshold-based methods.

the trade-offs between simplicity and diagnostic richness. Ultimately, we see our work
as complementary: while single-channel systems are suitable for screening, detailed
multi-channel models like ours offer higher resolution insights needed for personalized
interventions and advancing our understanding of sleep apnea pathophysiology.

seconds. We also considered transformer-based models but found them less suitable
for our mid-scale dataset due to their high parameter count and increased risk of

### Reviewer 1

This study focuses on detecting sleep apnea-related respiratory events through the use of a deep learning approach and up to 7 PSG overnight signals (plus data from EEG, EOG, and EMG). The topic is of interest for sleep research, the objectives are well-proposed, and the manuscript is well-written. The authors establish that their approach is useful in sleep apnea detection, mainly because of its ability to properly differentiate the several types of respiratory events (including a new event type), thus covering a gap in the related literature. Despite the interest of the proposal, it is my opinion that several major and minor issues should be addressed prior to the publication of the manuscript:
Major issues:
1/ Apneic event length is 10 seconds or more. Therefore, the frequency associated with their occurrence is below 0.1 Hz. Accordingly, respiratory signals being filtered between 0.1 Hz and 4 Hz are losing very important information. Several studies report that the most useful sleep apnea-related information in respiratory signals is below 0.1 Hz. It is my opinion that filtering should be changed to between 0.025 Hz and 4 Hz to improve the performance of the model, which is high but not impressive.
2/ I understand the advantages of the current proposal regarding previous approaches. However, it is my opinion that the manuscript fails to compare the diagnostic performance (not the scoring performance) with that reached by many other proposals. There exist previous studies using thousands of subjects but only using single channels like SpO2 that reach diagnostic performances that cannot be seen as inferior to those reported here using 7 + 3 signals. As diagnosis is the major conceptual goal of these automated approaches, the authors should compare and discuss these results with other relevant proposals in this particular task.
3/ As there are deep learning solutions that do not require an equal sample rate for the signals, and 8 Hz is below the sampling rate recommended by the AASM for respiratory signals, this choice should be justified and acknowledged as a limitation of the study.
4/ I think that the choice of the particular deep learning architecture should be justified and discussed. The existence of literature pointing to CNNs as reaching higher performances than RNNs, even in tasks involving signal processing (time series), justifies clearly explaining the reasons behind the choice of the deep learning architecture (which in this case includes a combination of both approaches via ResNet).
5/ The intra-class correlation coefficient is better suited than Pearson’s correlation to measure agreement between different scorers (with the predicted AHI being one of them).
Minor issues:
- "To simplify any annotated mixed apneas were labelled as OA due to there being an effort to breathe during the event." It is my opinion that this is not a simplification but a limitation (probably due to an unavoidable class imbalance concerning this type of event)

### Reviewer 2

The authors present an assessment of a new automatic sleep disordered breathing event detector (ABED) for identifying respiratory events in sleep disordered breathing. They report that generally the ABED performs as well as individual expert scores, particularly for obstructive apneic events. Data from a number of different, existing cohorts were used to train and validate the ABED, which is a strength of the study.
The potential of this is that the very rapid inference time (14 seconds per average PSG is cited) can increase efficiency and scope of sleep apnea testing.
A number of possible areas for clinical translation are given. I think the most attractive is in easily identifying endotypes of obstructive sleep apnea. Endotypic traits have been proposed for use in selecting patients that might benefit preferentially from a range of non-CPAP alternative therapies including oral appliances, hypoglossal nerve stimulation, supplemental oxygen, and pharmacotherapy. Given there is currently a one-size-fits-all management approach that predominates where CPAP is first line treatment for almost all patients. Accurately identifying patients likely to respond to alternatives to CPAP to avoid a trial and error approach to alternatives would be a major advance. Systems to identify endotypes from routine PSG signals with automated modelling have been developed and some are referenced here (21-25). However, the authors have not referenced further work that has demonstrated some of these systems are highly accurate in predicting, for example, oral appliance treatment outcomes in obstructive sleep apnea (see Dutta et al, J Clin Sleep Med 2022), or that combine clinical data and models from PSG data (see Eckert et al, Sleep 2024;47 (Suppl 1): A257) to identify successful candidates for Oral Appliance Therapy (and vice versa). The authors assert that the addition of “apnotyping” via probabilistic detection of event subtypes within each majority class could benefit sleep apnea endotyping. It remains an open question whether the ABED will be as effective as these methods in clinical practice as this should be acknowledged in the limitations. Further research is also needed to demonstrate if endotypes are useful in predicting which patients are at risk of adverse health consequences of OSA. This is beyond the scope of the current study.
The authors also do not reference previous work on the significance of isolated respiratory events without arousals or desaturations (IRE). Previous work has shown non-apneic REs without cortical arousal or desaturation are associated with significant respiratory and heart rate changes. And, that optimal CPAP and the reduction of resistive load are associated with the normalization of heart rate indicating potential clinical benefit (for example see Sankari et al, Sleep 2016 ;40:zsw024). Easy identification of these events would be useful but is not a novel finding.
There are a number of other limitations I feel need to be considered in addition to those given in the Discussion. As the authors point out in the Introduction, a number of novel metrics taken from the PSG have been identified that have shown to be better predictors of downstream consequences of OSA than the AHI. These include hypoxic burden and a number of metrics derived from heart rates. Further, the intensity of arousals from events are also likely to be clinically significant. It does not appear that the ABED identifies any of these metrics. Consequently, the value of the ABED in identifying which patients may benefit long-term from therapy is uncertain. Sleep studies also require scoring of sleep stages and identification of arousals due to limb movements or that occur spontaneously. I presume the ABED would need to be utilised in addition to automatic scoring software for these features.
Overall, the paper presents a potentially useful addition to automate the scoring of sleep-disordered breathing events that will likely be of value in sleep medicine.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This study focuses on detecting sleep apnea-related respiratory events through the use of a deep learning approach and up to 7 PSG overnight signals (plus data from EEG, EOG, and EMG). The topic is of interest for sleep research, the objectives are well-proposed, and the manuscript is well-written. The authors establish that their approach is useful in sleep apnea detection, mainly because of its ability to properly differentiate the several types of respiratory events (including a new event type), thus covering a gap in the related literature. Despite the interest of the proposal, it is my opinion that several major and minor issues should be addressed prior to the publication of the manuscript:
Major issues:
1/ Apneic event length is 10 seconds or more. Therefore, the frequency associated with their occurrence is below 0.1 Hz. Accordingly, respiratory signals being filtered between 0.1 Hz and 4 Hz are losing very important information. Several studies report that the most useful sleep apnea-related information in respiratory signals is below 0.1 Hz. It is my opinion that filtering should be changed to between 0.025 Hz and 4 Hz to improve the performance of the model, which is high but not impressive.

However, it is my opinion that the manuscript fails to compare the diagnostic performance (not the scoring performance) with that reached by many other proposals. There exist previous studies using thousands of subjects but only using single channels like SpO2 that reach diagnostic performances that cannot be seen as inferior to those reported here using 7 + 3 signals. As diagnosis is the major conceptual goal of these automated approaches, the authors should compare and discuss these results with other relevant proposals in this particular task.

### Reviewer 2

The authors present an assessment of a new automatic sleep disordered breathing event detector (ABED) for identifying respiratory events in sleep disordered breathing. They report that generally the ABED performs as well as individual expert scores, particularly for obstructive apneic events. Data from a number of different, existing cohorts were used to train and validate the ABED, which is a strength of the study.
The potential of this is that the very rapid inference time (14 seconds per average PSG is cited) can increase efficiency and scope of sleep apnea testing.
A number of possible areas for clinical translation are given. I think the most attractive is in easily identifying endotypes of obstructive sleep apnea. Endotypic traits have been proposed for use in selecting patients that might benefit preferentially from a range of non-CPAP alternative therapies including oral appliances, hypoglossal nerve stimulation, supplemental oxygen, and pharmacotherapy. Given there is currently a one-size-fits-all management approach that predominates where CPAP is first line treatment for almost all patients. Accurately identifying patients likely to respond to alternatives to CPAP to avoid a trial and error approach to alternatives would be a major advance. Systems to identify endotypes from routine PSG signals with automated modelling have been developed and some are referenced here (21-25). However, the authors have not referenced further work that has demonstrated some of these systems are highly accurate in predicting, for example, oral appliance treatment outcomes in obstructive sleep apnea (see Dutta et al, J Clin Sleep Med 2022), or that combine clinical data and models from PSG data (see Eckert et al, Sleep 2024;47 (Suppl 1): A257) to identify successful candidates for Oral Appliance Therapy (and vice versa). The authors assert that the addition of “apnotyping” via probabilistic detection of event subtypes within each majority class could benefit sleep apnea endotyping. It remains an open question whether the ABED will be as effective as these methods in clinical practice as this should be acknowledged in the limitations. Further research is also needed to demonstrate if endotypes are useful in predicting which patients are at risk of adverse health consequences of OSA. This is beyond the scope of the current study.
The authors also do not reference previous work on the significance of isolated respiratory events without arousals or desaturations (IRE). Previous work has shown non-apneic REs without cortical arousal or desaturation are associated with significant respiratory and heart rate changes. And, that optimal CPAP and the reduction of resistive load are associated with the normalization of heart rate indicating potential clinical benefit (for example see Sankari et al, Sleep 2016 ;40:zsw024). Easy identification of these events would be useful but is not a novel finding.
There are a number of other limitations I feel need to be considered in addition to those given in the Discussion. As the authors point out in the Introduction, a number of novel metrics taken from the PSG have been identified that have shown to be better predictors of downstream consequences of OSA than the AHI. These include hypoxic burden and a number of metrics derived from heart rates. Further, the intensity of arousals from events are also likely to be clinically significant. It does not appear that the ABED identifies any of these metrics. Consequently, the value of the ABED in identifying which patients may benefit long-term from therapy is uncertain. Sleep studies also require scoring of sleep stages and identification of arousals due to limb movements or that occur spontaneously. I presume the ABED would need to be utilised in addition to automatic scoring software for these features.
Overall, the paper presents a potentially useful addition to automate the scoring of sleep-disordered breathing events that will likely be of value in sleep medicine.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), particularly residual networks (ResNets), are

cohorts were used to train and validate the ABED, which is a strength of the study.

is cited) can increase efficiency and scope of sleep apnea testing.
A number of possible areas for clinical translation are given. I think the most attractive is
in easily identifying endotypes of obstructive sleep apnea. Endotypic traits have been
proposed for use in selecting patients that might benefit preferentially from a range of
non-CPAP alternative therapies including oral appliances, hypoglossal nerve
stimulation, supplemental oxygen, and pharmacotherapy. Given there is currently a
one-size-fits-all management approach that predominates where CPAP is first line
treatment for almost all patients. Accurately identifying patients likely to respond to
alternatives to CPAP to avoid a trial and error approach to alternatives would be a major
advance. Systems to identify endotypes from routine PSG signals with automated
modelling have been developed and some are referenced here (21-25). However, the
authors have not referenced further work that has demonstrated some of these systems
are highly accurate in predicting, for example, oral appliance treatment outcomes in
obstructive sleep apnea (see Dutta et al, J Clin Sleep Med 2022), or that combine
clinical data and models from PSG data (see Eckert et al, Sleep 2024;47 (Suppl 1):
A257) to identify successful candidates for Oral Appliance Therapy (and vice versa).
We thank the reviewer for highlighting the clinical relevance of endotype-based
treatment selection and for suggesting key references that strengthen the translational
potential of our work. In our revised manuscript, we have incorporated the study by
Dutta et al. (2022) [https://jcsm.aasm.org/doi/full/10.5664/jcsm.9742], which developed
a physiological-based model using standard polysomnography and clinical data to
predict oral appliance treatment outcomes in obstructive sleep apnea. This study
reported a mean accuracy of 91% ± 8% using 10-fold cross-validation and 100%
accuracy in an independent validation set for predicting responders (AHI < 5 events/h)
PMC. We have also referenced the work by Eckert et al. (2024)
[https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/47/Supplement_1/A257/7654650?login=true],

appliance therapy. These additions provide a more comprehensive overview of existing
predictive models in the field.

subtypes within each majority class could benefit sleep apnea endotyping. It remains an
open question whether the ABED will be as effective as these methods in clinical
practice as this should be acknowledged in the limitations. Further research is also
needed to demonstrate if endotypes are useful in predicting which patients are at risk of
adverse health consequences of OSA. This is beyond the scope of the current study.
We acknowledge that while the ABED demonstrates promising performance in
detecting respiratory events and subtypes, its effectiveness in predicting treatment
outcomes, such as response to oral appliance therapy, remains to be established. In the
revised manuscript, we have added a statement in the limitations section to reflect this,
noting that further research is needed to compare the ABED's predictive capabilities
with existing models and to validate its clinical utility in diverse patient populations.

respiratory events without arousals or desaturations (IRE). Previous work has shown
non-apneic REs without cortical arousal or desaturation are associated with significant
respiratory and heart rate changes. And, that optimal CPAP and the reduction of
resistive load are associated with the normalization of heart rate indicating potential
clinical benefit (for example see Sankari et al, Sleep 2016 ;40:zsw024). Easy
identification of these events would be useful but is not a novel finding.

by Sankari et al. (2016), which demonstrated that non-apneic respiratory events without
cortical arousal or desaturation are associated with significant respiratory and heart rate
changes, and that optimal CPAP therapy can normalize heart rate, indicating potential
clinical benefit. This addition acknowledges the clinical significance of IREs and situates
our work within the broader context of sleep-disordered breathing research.

given in the Discussion. As the authors point out in the Introduction, a number of novel
metrics taken from the PSG have been identified that have shown to be better
predictors of downstream consequences of OSA than the AHI. These include hypoxic
burden and a number of metrics derived from heart rates. Further, the intensity of
arousals from events are also likely to be clinically significant. It does not appear that
the ABED identifies any of these metrics. Consequently, the value of the ABED in
identifying which patients may benefit long-term from therapy is uncertain. Sleep studies
also require scoring of sleep stages and identification of arousals due to limb
movements or that occur spontaneously. I presume the ABED would need to be utilised
in addition to automatic scoring software for these features.

manuscript, we have expanded the limitations section to discuss the following points:

acknowledge that the ABED does not identify certain novel metrics derived from
PSG, such as hypoxic burden and heart rate variability, which have been shown
to be better predictors of downstream consequences of OSA than the AHI
[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8483223/?,
https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/40/14/1149/5146754].

scoring of sleep stages and identification of arousals due to limb movements or
spontaneous occurrences. The ABED is designed to detect respiratory events
and would need to be utilized in conjunction with automated scoring tools for full
PSG interpretation.
These acknowledgments provide a more balanced perspective on the capabilities and
current limitations of the ABED system.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This study focuses on detecting sleep apnea-related respiratory events through the use of a deep learning approach and up to 7 PSG overnight signals (plus data from EEG, EOG, and EMG). The topic is of interest for sleep research, the objectives are well-proposed, and the manuscript is well-written. The authors establish that their approach is useful in sleep apnea detection, mainly because of its ability to properly differentiate the several types of respiratory events (including a new event type), thus covering a gap in the related literature. Despite the interest of the proposal, it is my opinion that several major and minor issues should be addressed prior to the publication of the manuscript:
Major issues:
1/ Apneic event length is 10 seconds or more. Therefore, the frequency associated with their occurrence is below 0.1 Hz. Accordingly, respiratory signals being filtered between 0.1 Hz and 4 Hz are losing very important information. Several studies report that the most useful sleep apnea-related information in respiratory signals is below 0.1 Hz. It is my opinion that filtering should be changed to between 0.025 Hz and 4 Hz to improve the performance of the model, which is high but not impressive.
2/ I understand the advantages of the current proposal regarding previous approaches. However, it is my opinion that the manuscript fails to compare the diagnostic performance (not the scoring performance) with that reached by many other proposals. There exist previous studies using thousands of subjects but only using single channels like SpO2 that reach diagnostic performances that cannot be seen as inferior to those reported here using 7 + 3 signals. As diagnosis is the major conceptual goal of these automated approaches, the authors should compare and discuss these results with other relevant proposals in this particular task.
3/ As there are deep learning solutions that do not require an equal sample rate for the signals, and 8 Hz is below the sampling rate recommended by the AASM for respiratory signals, this choice should be justified and acknowledged as a limitation of the study.
4/ I think that the choice of the particular deep learning architecture should be justified and discussed. The existence of literature pointing to CNNs as reaching higher performances than RNNs, even in tasks involving signal processing (time series), justifies clearly explaining the reasons behind the choice of the deep learning architecture (which in this case includes a combination of both approaches via ResNet).
5/ The intra-class correlation coefficient is better suited than Pearson’s correlation to measure agreement between different scorers (with the predicted AHI being one of them).
Minor issues:
- "To simplify any annotated mixed apneas were labelled as OA due to there being an effort to breathe during the event." It is my opinion that this is not a simplification but a limitation (probably due to an unavoidable class imbalance concerning this type of event)

### Reviewer 2

The authors present an assessment of a new automatic sleep disordered breathing event detector (ABED) for identifying respiratory events in sleep disordered breathing. They report that generally the ABED performs as well as individual expert scores, particularly for obstructive apneic events. Data from a number of different, existing cohorts were used to train and validate the ABED, which is a strength of the study.
The potential of this is that the very rapid inference time (14 seconds per average PSG is cited) can increase efficiency and scope of sleep apnea testing.
A number of possible areas for clinical translation are given. I think the most attractive is in easily identifying endotypes of obstructive sleep apnea. Endotypic traits have been proposed for use in selecting patients that might benefit preferentially from a range of non-CPAP alternative therapies including oral appliances, hypoglossal nerve stimulation, supplemental oxygen, and pharmacotherapy. Given there is currently a one-size-fits-all management approach that predominates where CPAP is first line treatment for almost all patients. Accurately identifying patients likely to respond to alternatives to CPAP to avoid a trial and error approach to alternatives would be a major advance. Systems to identify endotypes from routine PSG signals with automated modelling have been developed and some are referenced here (21-25). However, the authors have not referenced further work that has demonstrated some of these systems are highly accurate in predicting, for example, oral appliance treatment outcomes in obstructive sleep apnea (see Dutta et al, J Clin Sleep Med 2022), or that combine clinical data and models from PSG data (see Eckert et al, Sleep 2024;47 (Suppl 1): A257) to identify successful candidates for Oral Appliance Therapy (and vice versa). The authors assert that the addition of “apnotyping” via probabilistic detection of event subtypes within each majority class could benefit sleep apnea endotyping. It remains an open question whether the ABED will be as effective as these methods in clinical practice as this should be acknowledged in the limitations. Further research is also needed to demonstrate if endotypes are useful in predicting which patients are at risk of adverse health consequences of OSA. This is beyond the scope of the current study.
The authors also do not reference previous work on the significance of isolated respiratory events without arousals or desaturations (IRE). Previous work has shown non-apneic REs without cortical arousal or desaturation are associated with significant respiratory and heart rate changes. And, that optimal CPAP and the reduction of resistive load are associated with the normalization of heart rate indicating potential clinical benefit (for example see Sankari et al, Sleep 2016 ;40:zsw024). Easy identification of these events would be useful but is not a novel finding.
There are a number of other limitations I feel need to be considered in addition to those given in the Discussion. As the authors point out in the Introduction, a number of novel metrics taken from the PSG have been identified that have shown to be better predictors of downstream consequences of OSA than the AHI. These include hypoxic burden and a number of metrics derived from heart rates. Further, the intensity of arousals from events are also likely to be clinically significant. It does not appear that the ABED identifies any of these metrics. Consequently, the value of the ABED in identifying which patients may benefit long-term from therapy is uncertain. Sleep studies also require scoring of sleep stages and identification of arousals due to limb movements or that occur spontaneously. I presume the ABED would need to be utilised in addition to automatic scoring software for these features.
Overall, the paper presents a potentially useful addition to automate the scoring of sleep-disordered breathing events that will likely be of value in sleep medicine.

The authors assert that the addition of “apnotyping” via probabilistic detection of event
subtypes within each majority class could benefit sleep apnea endotyping. It remains an
open question whether the ABED will be as effective as these methods in clinical
practice as this should be acknowledged in the limitations. Further research is also
needed to demonstrate if endotypes are useful in predicting which patients are at risk of
adverse health consequences of OSA. This is beyond the scope of the current study.
We acknowledge that while the ABED demonstrates promising performance in
detecting respiratory events and subtypes, its effectiveness in predicting treatment
outcomes, such as response to oral appliance therapy, remains to be established. In the
revised manuscript, we have added a statement in the limitations section to reflect this,
noting that further research is needed to compare the ABED's predictive capabilities
with existing models and to validate its clinical utility in diverse patient populations.
The authors also do not reference previous work on the significance of isolated
respiratory events without arousals or desaturations (IRE). Previous work has shown
non-apneic REs without cortical arousal or desaturation are associated with significant
respiratory and heart rate changes. And, that optimal CPAP and the reduction of
resistive load are associated with the normalization of heart rate indicating potential
clinical benefit (for example see Sankari et al, Sleep 2016 ;40:zsw024). Easy
identification of these events would be useful but is not a novel finding.
Thank you for highlighting this omission. We have now included a reference to the study
by Sankari et al. (2016), which demonstrated that non-apneic respiratory events without
cortical arousal or desaturation are associated with significant respiratory and heart rate
changes, and that optimal CPAP therapy can normalize heart rate, indicating potential
clinical benefit. This addition acknowledges the clinical significance of IREs and situates
our work within the broader context of sleep-disordered breathing research.
There are a number of other limitations I feel need to be considered in addition to those
given in the Discussion. As the authors point out in the Introduction, a number of novel
metrics taken from the PSG have been identified that have shown to be better
predictors of downstream consequences of OSA than the AHI. These include hypoxic
burden and a number of metrics derived from heart rates. Further, the intensity of
arousals from events are also likely to be clinically significant. It does not appear that
the ABED identifies any of these metrics. Consequently, the value of the ABED in
identifying which patients may benefit long-term from therapy is uncertain. Sleep studies
also require scoring of sleep stages and identification of arousals due to limb
movements or that occur spontaneously. I presume the ABED would need to be utilised
in addition to automatic scoring software for these features.
We appreciate the reviewer’s insights into additional limitations. In the revised
manuscript, we have expanded the limitations section to discuss the following points:
● Novel Metrics: Although ABED describes the overall apnotypes of subjects, we
acknowledge that the ABED does not identify certain novel metrics derived from
PSG, such as hypoxic burden and heart rate variability, which have been shown
to be better predictors of downstream consequences of OSA than the AHI
[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8483223/?,
https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/40/14/1149/5146754].
● Comprehensive Sleep Study Scoring: We recognize that sleep studies require
scoring of sleep stages and identification of arousals due to limb movements or
spontaneous occurrences. The ABED is designed to detect respiratory events
and would need to be utilized in conjunction with automated scoring tools for full
PSG interpretation.
These acknowledgments provide a more balanced perspective on the capabilities and
current limitations of the ABED system.
